name: Utah

events.title: Statehood
events.text: Utah became the 45th state on January 4, 1896. Congress gave it 1 seat in the House until the next apportionment.

events.title: 1900 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1900 census, Utah kept 1 seat in the House. It elected its one member statewide (at-large).

events.title: 1910 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1910 census, Utah's House delegation grew from 1 to 2 seats.

events.title: Statewide (general ticket) elections
events.text: In the 63rd Congress (1913–1915), Utah elected all of its representatives statewide on a general ticket instead of by district.

events.title: 1930 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1930 census, Utah kept 2 seats in the House.

events.title: 1940 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1940 census, Utah kept 2 seats in the House.

events.title: 1950 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1950 census, Utah kept 2 seats in the House.

events.title: 1960 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1960 census, Utah kept 2 seats in the House.

events.title: 1970 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1970 census, Utah kept 2 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1980 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1980 census, Utah's House delegation grew from 2 to 3 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 1990 census apportionment
events.text: After the 1990 census, Utah kept 3 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2000 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2000 census, Utah kept 3 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: 2010 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2010 census, Utah's House delegation grew from 3 to 4 seats. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: Proposition 4
events.text: Utah voters approved Proposition 4, creating an independent commission to recommend maps and setting standards for drawing them.

events.title: 2020 census apportionment
events.text: After the 2020 census, Utah kept 4 seats in the House. Because districts must have nearly equal populations, the map was redrawn with the new census counts.

events.title: League of Women Voters v. Utah State Legislature
events.text: The Utah Supreme Court ruled in July 2024 that the legislature's changes to the voter-approved Proposition 4 could be challenged under the state constitution, and sent the case back to the trial court.

events.title: Court-ordered map
events.text: A state judge struck down the 2021 congressional map in August 2025. In November she rejected the legislature's replacement and adopted a map proposed by the plaintiffs, with one district centered on northern Salt Lake County, which the 2021 map had split four ways. In February 2026 the Utah Supreme Court declined to reinstate the 2021 map, and the court-ordered map was used in 2026.

compactnessNote: Polsby-Popper compactness (4π × area ÷ perimeter²) measured on the projected district shapes. It describes shape only: coastlines, rivers and county lines lower it too, so a low score is not evidence of intent. "Irregular" marks the least compact 5% of district shapes in each census era nationally.

c064.text: New map drawn after the 1910 census, which raised Utah's seats from 1 to 2. It was first used in the 1914 election.

c090.text: Utah's district lines were redrawn between censuses, first used in the 1966 election. The reason has not been researched yet.

c093.text: New map drawn after the 1970 census, which left Utah with 2 seats. It was first used in the 1972 election.

c098.text: New map drawn after the 1980 census, which raised Utah's seats from 2 to 3. It was first used in the 1982 election.

c103.text: New map drawn after the 1990 census, which left Utah with 3 seats. It was first used in the 1992 election.

c108.text: New map drawn after the 2000 census, which left Utah with 3 seats. It was first used in the 2002 election.

c113.text: New map drawn after the 2010 census, which raised Utah's seats from 3 to 4. It was first used in the 2012 election.

c118.text: New map drawn after the 2020 census, which left Utah with 4 seats. It was first used in the 2022 election.

In November she rejected the legislature's replacement and adopted a map proposed by the plaintiffs, with one district centered on northern Salt Lake County, which the 2021 map had split four ways. In February 2026 the Utah Supreme Court declined to reinstate the 2021 map, and the court-ordered map was used in 2026.
